title: Arjuna's austerities
hook: Shiva gives Arjuna his own weapon with a warning, the guardians of the world add theirs, and a chariot comes down for him
carry: use only as much as you need

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities ended in a lost fight and a garland on the hunter's head. Your line was stop pushing, offer something instead. Did you stop pushing in one struggle, and offer something instead? Day seven hundred eighty-six.
screen: `ARJUNA'S AUSTERITIES.` · `THE GARLAND ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.`

segments.voice: What does a god give a man who just tried to kill him? Arjuna is on his knees, bruised, asking forgiveness. The hunter's disguise has fallen away, and Shiva stands before him with Uma at his side. And the first thing Shiva does isn't a lecture. He hands back the bow. Gandiva, the one he snatched in the fight, is returned to Arjuna's hands. Then Shiva says: ask for what you want. Today, the gift at the end of Arjuna's austerities, and the warning that comes with it.
screen: `WHAT DOES A GOD GIVE?` → `SHIVA HANDS BACK THE BOW.` → `ASK FOR WHAT YOU WANT.`

segments.voice: There's no anger in Shiva at all. And he touches Arjuna, and his wounds and his exhaustion are gone. Then Arjuna asks for what he climbed the mountain for. He asks for Shiva's own weapon, the one called Pashupata. Shiva gives it to him, and teaches him how to use it. But he adds a warning, and it's the heart of the scene. This weapon, he says, must never be hurled at a human foe, and never at a weaker one. Used wrongly, it could destroy the world. Shiva's own weapon comes with Shiva's own limit. And then the sky fills with visitors. The guardians of the world arrive one after another: Varuna, lord of the waters; Kubera, lord of wealth; Yama, lord of death; each offering Arjuna a weapon of his own. Last comes Indra, the father who tested him in disguise at the start of all this. Indra tells him a chariot will come for him, to carry him up to Indra's own city, where he will receive more. So the whole arc of Arjuna's austerities comes into view. He set out holding a purpose, and wouldn't put it down. He burned with tapas until the mountain felt it. He met Shiva as a stranger, lost to him, and recognized him through his own offering. And what he receives at the end isn't only power. It's power with a rule attached, given by a god who first healed the man who had fought him.
screen: `SHIVA HEALS AND PRAISES ARJUNA.` · `THE PASHUPATA WEAPON.` · `NEVER AGAINST A WEAKER FOE.` · then, large: `THE GUARDIANS OF THE WORLD ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and feel the breath move in and out. Bring to mind one strength you have: a skill, a sharp tongue, a position, a way with people. Breathe in, and receive it as a gift. Breathe out, and hear Shiva's warning: never against someone weaker. Where might that strength need a limit? Let that question sit with you, no judgment, just attention. If you pray, you can give thanks for that gift and ask to use it well. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. They end with healing, the Pashupata weapon from Shiva, and a warning never to turn it on the weak.
Your line: use only as much as you need. Today, when you have the upper hand with someone, use only as much of it as you need. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: In Hindu storytelling, Shiva's gift of the Pashupata weapon to Arjuna is remembered together with its warning, and the episode is honored by devotees of Shiva as a sign of the god's grace to a devoted seeker.

myth: Shiva punished Arjuna for fighting him
he praised him, healed him and offered him a boon.
Shiva warned that the Pashupata must never be used against a weaker foe
used wrongly, he said, it could destroy the world.
Shiva was the only god to give Arjuna a weapon on the mountain
the guardians of the world came and gave him weapons too.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. Shiva, whom you just fought, tells you to ask for anything. what do you ask for?
options: to go home to your brothers.
fork.reveal: he asks for the Pashupata, and Shiva gives it, with a strict warning about how it may be used.

original.note: Sanskrit pāśupata: belonging to Pashupati, 'lord of creatures', a name of Shiva; the name of his weapon.

trapdoor: what you thought: Arjuna got the ultimate weapon as a prize.
what it means: Shiva gave it with a strict limit, never against a weaker foe, or it could destroy the world.
what a scholar hears: the gift comes from Pashupati, a name of Shiva, and it ends the mountain ordeal by sending Arjuna on to Indra's city.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Kairata Parva (Shiva returns Gandiva, heals Arjuna, grants the Pashupata with a warning; the guardians of the world give weapons; Indra promises a chariot)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli that Shiva returns Gandiva, touches and heals Arjuna, and gives the Pashupata (Ganguli may also call it Brahmasira); confirm the wording of the warning (not to be hurled at foes of little might, lest it destroy the universe).
Confirm which guardians of the world come (Varuna, Kubera, Yama, Indra) and what each gives, and that Indra promises Matali's chariot to take Arjuna to heaven.

Editor: replaced the superlative 'the greatest gift comes with the strictest limit' with 'Shiva's own weapon comes with Shiva's own limit'; 'met God as a stranger' changed to 'met Shiva' so the narrator doesn't speak as a believer; varied the 'look at' opener.
Original: pashupata as 'of Pashupati' is standard Sanskrit; Keeper to confirm under the etymology rule.
Day 787 (another writer) opens in Indra's city; this close leaves Arjuna on the edge of that journey.

Audit: Ganguli's warning is that the weapon must not be hurled at men, and if hurled at one of little might it could destroy the universe; the human-foe clause was missing and is now added. Cut the repeat of Shiva praising Arjuna's fighting, already the close of day 785.
